claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
In the past, having more choices usually meant more complexity and technical debt.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.

A GeoDeploy deployment request consists of target geos (traffic share and data-residency rule: EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape, and constraints (allowed providers, provider count, budget).
In GeoDeploy, Jev never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; the TypeScript app does all math; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS and decides nothing.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters instance types by image architecture, and computes monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
The Pulumi Automation API runs a preview and then an update with one stack per region, and GeoDeploy won't run unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The link /automation/ points to a valid Pulumi Automation API page.
Every GeoDeploy run writes plan.json and plan.md and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.

Jev exposes three primitives: choice() returns the pick, a probability distribution across options, and a confidence; score() rates against a rubric (GeoDeploy uses 10 levels); noul() answers yes/no with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates in a single call.
GeoDeploy asks Jev for one selection, five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard noul checks (residency, capacity), and a fallback choice.
The @typesafe-ai/sdk package exports choice, noul, and score, and provides TypeSafeClient with a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers.
TypeSafe's advice for rubrics is to "describe situations, not degrees."
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.

Weight profile values: latency-optimized cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12; balanced 0.25/0.25/0.2/0.12/0.18; residency-first 0.12/0.12/0.38/0.23/0.15; failure-domain 0.08/0.17/0.48/0.15/0.12.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow from the provider, and Jev decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human); region with existing stack 0.75 (keep existing); ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 (drop AI path for geo).
The residency check is in packages/decide/src/engine.ts and question definitions are in packages/decide/src/questions.ts in the GeoDeploy repo.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy falls back to deterministic price comparison across providers while enforcing residency and constraint checks; `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.

In self-driving mode (`geodeploy monitor`), the agent periodically checks CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question with options no-change, scale-up, scale-down, or shift, plus a disruption-risk check; code computes node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically, between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval, and below 0.70 GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic per-region rule.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as latency and error rates.
GeoDeploy is open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
Pulumi's X account handle is @PulumiCorp.
